problem: It says the resolution advisory 'drives the autopilot'. In TCAS II the RA is a command shown to the crew on the flight director and vertical-speed indicator, and the pilot must fly it; the autopilot is normally disengaged during an RA and is never commanded by TCAS.
fix: TCAS II shows its resolution advisory as a commanded climb or descent rate on the flight director and vertical-speed indicator. The crew must respond within a few seconds; the autopilot is normally disconnected, not driven by the RA.

problem: One 112-bit extended squitter does not carry position, altitude, velocity and identity together. Position with altitude, velocity, and identity (callsign) travel in separate message types, sent in turn.
fix: About twice a second the aircraft sends extended squitters on 1090 MHz: 112-bit messages that between them carry its GNSS position and altitude, its velocity, and its identity.

problem: FIS-B weather is broadcast on the 978 MHz UAT data link, not on 1090 MHz extended squitter, so 'ADS-B In receives ... weather (FIS-B)' is too general.
fix: ADS-B In receives traffic and ground-uplinked radar tracks (TIS-B); on the UAT data link it also receives weather (FIS-B).

problem: The example uses 1030 MHz as the transmit frequency of a primary pulse radar, which is the SSR ground-interrogation frequency the chapter warns about. A student may read it as a rule that primary radars transmit at 1030 MHz.
fix: Add one line: 1030 MHz is picked here only to practise the arithmetic; a primary surveillance radar transmits elsewhere in L-band, and 1030 MHz belongs to the SSR interrogation uplink.
